query: High-entropy alloys contain five or more elements at 5–35 at% each, generally with comparable atomic radii. Refractory and nickel-based high-entropy alloys have demonstrated elevated-temperature mechanical properties comparable to titanium- and nickel-based alloys used in extreme environments because of their heat resistance and specific strength. However, prior investigations have mainly treated titanium and nickel as additions, leaving alloys in which both are primary constituents unexplored. Subject to the stated compositional definition, what single testable intervention hypothesis could improve the elevated-temperature mechanical properties of a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy relative to the same material without the intervention? Specify the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted relative outcome, composition and operating boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment with explicit results that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In a titanium‐ and nickel‐primary high-entropy alloy (e.g., Ti40Ni40Cr10Al5V5), incorporating a controlled trace addition of reactive yttrium oxide precursors (optimally around 1 wt%, within 0.5–2 wt%) during mechanical alloying followed by spark plasma sintering under a reducing atmosphere will lead to the in-situ formation of a uniform dispersion of nanoscale Y2O3 particles. These particles will act as barriers to dislocation motion and grain boundary sliding at elevated temperatures, thereby enhancing the alloy’s yield strength and creep resistance relative to an equivalent alloy processed without the yttrium oxide addition.
generation.material_initial_state: A conventionally processed titanium‐ and nickel‐primary high-entropy alloy (e.g., Ti40Ni40Cr10Al5V5) produced by mechanical alloying and consolidation without any reactive oxide precursor.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled trace addition of reactive yttrium oxide precursors (~0.5–2 wt%, optimally ~1 wt%) during the mechanical alloying of the elemental powders, followed by spark plasma sintering under a reducing atmosphere to facilitate in-situ formation of Y2O3 dispersoids.
generation.conditions: Mechanical alloying of the base elements with the yttrium oxide precursor, then spark plasma sintering at 1100–1200 °C under a reducing atmosphere to prevent unwanted oxidation and ensure the formation of a homogeneous, nanoscale Y2O3 dispersion.
generation.structural_mediator: A uniform dispersion of nanometer-scale Y2O3 oxide particles embedded within the alloy’s dendritic or solid-solution matrix.
generation.mechanism: The thermally stable Y2O3 dispersoids impede dislocation motion and restrict grain boundary sliding, effectively raising the yield strength and enhancing creep resistance at elevated temperatures by pinning microstructural features.
generation.predicted_outcome: The intervention is expected to yield a significant increase in high-temperature yield strength and improved creep resistance compared to the baseline alloy processed without yttrium oxide addition. The exact magnitude of improvement is uncertain and will depend on the achieved uniformity and stability of the dispersoids.
generation.baseline: The same titanium‐ and nickel‐primary HEA processed without the incorporation of yttrium oxide precursors, exhibiting typical elevated-temperature mechanical properties without oxide dispersion strengthening.
generation.boundary: This effect is anticipated in alloys with compositions meeting high-entropy criteria (e.g., Ti40Ni40Cr10Al5V5) and is effective under elevated temperatures typically above 600 °C. The yttrium oxide addition must remain in the controlled range (0.5–2 wt%) to maintain the HEA composition and avoid deleterious effects.
generation.uncertainty: There remains uncertainty regarding the precise control over the uniformity of the Y2O3 dispersoid distribution and their long-term stability during prolonged high-temperature exposure. Detailed processing optimization and extensive microstructural characterization are required to resolve these uncertainties.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloy samples from an identical batch of Ti40Ni40Cr10Al5V5: one set with the controlled yttrium oxide precursor addition (using the optimized processing parameters) and a control set without the addition. Both sets will undergo the same mechanical alloying and optimized spark plasma sintering under a reducing atmosphere.
measurements: Perform high-temperature tensile tests (e.g., at 600–800 °C) to measure yield strength and ductility.
Conduct creep tests at a fixed load over time to assess creep resistance.
Use transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to evaluate the dispersion, size, and stability of Y2O3 nanoparticles before and after high-temperature exposure.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples containing Y2O3 do not demonstrate a statistically significant improvement in high-temperature yield strength and/or creep resistance compared to the control samples, or if TEM analysis reveals that the Y2O3 dispersoids are absent, non-uniform, or have significantly coarsened during high-temperature testing—thereby negating their expected strengthening effect—the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

proposals.material_system: A titanium‐ and nickel‐primary high-entropy alloy, e.g., Ti40Ni40Al10V5Cr5 (at%), meeting the HEA compositional definition
proposals.intervention: Introduce a controlled aging heat treatment to induce fine, uniformly dispersed nano‐precipitates (e.g., sigma phase or ordered intermetallics) within the primary BCC/dendritic matrix
proposals.conditions: Solutionize the as-cast alloy at ~1100 °C to homogenize, then age at 750–850 °C for 2–5 hours in an inert atmosphere
proposals.structural_mediator: Formation of nanometer-scale sigma precipitates at a uniform distribution inside the matrix
proposals.mechanism: The precipitates act as barriers to dislocation motion at elevated temperatures by impeding dislocation glide and creep deformation, thereby providing precipitation strengthening
proposals.predicted_outcome: An increase in yield strength and creep resistance at temperatures above 600 °C relative to the baseline alloy without the aging treatment
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: By deliberately inducing and controlling nanoscale precipitates in a Ti-Ni primary HEA, the alloy’s microstructure is engineered to resist high-temperature deformation, directly addressing the challenge of improving elevated-temperature mechanical properties in an unexplored composition where both titanium and nickel are primary constituents

proposals.material_system: A titanium‐ and nickel‐primary high-entropy alloy set (e.g., Ti40Ni40Cr10Al5V5) with minor reactive additions
proposals.intervention: Incorporate a controlled trace addition of reactive yttrium oxide precursors (~0.5–2 wt%) during mechanical alloying to form an oxide dispersion strengthened (ODS) microstructure upon consolidation
proposals.conditions: Mechanically alloy the mixed elemental powders followed by spark plasma sintering at 1100–1200 °C under a reducing atmosphere to prevent excessive oxidation while enabling in-situ formation of nanoscale Y2O3 dispersoids
proposals.structural_mediator: Uniform dispersion of fine, stable Y2O3 oxide particles within the dendritic/solid solution matrix
proposals.mechanism: The thermally stable oxide particles impede dislocation movement and grain boundary sliding at elevated temperatures via particle pinning effects, thereby increasing high-temperature strength and creep resistance
proposals.predicted_outcome: Enhanced elevated-temperature yield strength and improved creep resistance compared to an otherwise identical alloy processed without the Y2O3 addition
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This intervention leverages oxide dispersion strengthening—a proven mechanism in high-temperature alloys—to specifically stabilize the microstructure of a Ti-Ni primary HEA, countering diffusion-mediated softening at high temperatures

proposals.material_system: An equiatomic or near-equiatomic Ti-Ni-based HEA (e.g., Ti35Ni35Al15V10, with additional minor elements to meet HEA criteria)
proposals.intervention: Apply severe plastic deformation via equal-channel angular pressing (ECAP) followed by a rapid sub-transus annealing treatment
proposals.conditions: Deform the as-cast alloy using ECAP at ~500 °C (multiple passes to achieve significant grain refinement) then perform a rapid annealing at ~800 °C for 2 minutes to relieve internal stresses while retaining ultrafine grains
proposals.structural_mediator: An ultrafine-grained microstructure with high-angle grain boundaries
proposals.mechanism: Grain refinement strengthens the alloy through grain-boundary strengthening (Hall-Petch effect) and limits grain boundary sliding and diffusional creep at elevated temperatures
proposals.predicted_outcome: A significant increase (e.g., ~20–30% improvement) in high-temperature yield strength and/or creep resistance compared to the baseline coarse-grained alloy
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: By refining the microstructure the intervention enhances the high-temperature mechanical behavior of a Ti-Ni primary HEA without changing its chemical composition, offering an alternative processing route to improve performance in extreme environments

proposals.material_system: A titanium‐and nickel‐dominant HEA (for instance, Ti40Ni40Mo10Co5Fe5, where Mo, Co, and Fe are minor constituents to satisfy HEA criteria)
proposals.intervention: Introduce nanoscale deformation-induced twins via a cryogenic rolling process followed by a brief anneal to stabilize the twin boundaries
proposals.conditions: Perform rolling at liquid nitrogen temperature to promote high-density twin formation, then anneal rapidly at 600 °C for 1–2 minutes to recrystallize slightly without eliminating the twins
proposals.structural_mediator: High density of nanotwins and twin boundaries within the matrix
proposals.mechanism: Twin boundaries act as additional barriers to dislocation motion and contribute to both strength and ductility at elevated temperatures by accommodating deformation without extensive recovery
proposals.predicted_outcome: Improved strength and ductility at high temperatures (e.g., a notable increase in yield strength while maintaining or slightly improving plastic strain) relative to a conventionally processed, twin-free baseline alloy
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This approach exploits deformation-induced microstructural engineering specific to high-entropy alloys, targeting the enhancement of elevated-temperature mechanical properties in a system where titanium and nickel are primary constituents, an area that has remained largely unexplored
